label: Self-hosted incident management
headline: Bring incident operations onto your infrastructure.
description: Keep operational data and deployment decisions under your control. Connect alerts to on-call, response, customer updates and postmortems.
problem: You need a complete response workflow and the ability to decide where the system runs.
workflow: Deploy an integrated runtime, connect an inbound provider, configure schedules and routing, then validate one synthetic incident end to end.
deployment: Start with integrated Docker Compose when a single application host is acceptable. Move to split runtime or Kubernetes when availability, workload isolation, or independent scaling requires it.
integration: Connect one release-verified inbound provider first, map it to the owning service, then add ChatOps or issue-tracking only after the core alert-to-response path is proven.
security: Set the public HTTPS origin, durable PostgreSQL and backups, production secrets, and the identity policy before exposing the installation to responders.
validation: Run a synthetic incident through ingestion, correlation, on-call resolution, paging, acknowledgement, customer communication, resolution, and follow-up.

label: SRE teams
headline: Close the loop on reliability.
description: Connect the alert to the response, the response to the review, and the review to owned follow-up work.
problem: A restored service is only part of the job. Response evidence and learning need to survive the incident.
workflow: Track incident ownership and SLA outcomes, review MTTA and MTTR, and create a postmortem with action items assigned to owners.
deployment: Choose the smallest topology that still meets the reliability target for the incident platform itself; split runtime only where failure isolation or independent worker scaling is justified.
integration: Start with the monitoring systems that already define service health, then connect Slack or Teams for response collaboration and Jira when follow-up work belongs in the issue tracker.
security: Use scoped roles, audit evidence, and enterprise identity where required. Keep incident and postmortem data within the deployment boundary your team operates.
validation: Exercise one real service journey and verify MTTA/MTTR evidence, timeline completeness, postmortem creation, and owned action items after recovery.

label: Platform engineering
headline: Build a shared response foundation.
description: Give service teams a common incident workflow while keeping deployment, identity and operational health in view.
problem: Different teams own different services, but the incident platform still needs coherent access and operational control.
workflow: Organize teams and services, connect OIDC and SCIM, and use worker health and delivery evidence to operate the platform.
deployment: Standardize a supported deployment pattern for service teams, including database ownership, ingress, secrets, backups, health signals, and upgrade responsibility.
integration: Offer a curated set of monitoring and ChatOps paths instead of letting every team invent a different response contract. Use the generic webhook only for internal systems without a first-class provider.
security: Define OIDC/SCIM ownership, RBAC boundaries, auditor access, API-key scope, and session policy as part of the platform contract.
validation: Onboard a pilot service, trigger a synthetic incident, verify responder routing and delivery evidence, then validate Health Center and recovery procedures.

label: Regulated environments
headline: Keep control and evidence together.
description: Run the data plane yourself. Apply identity and authorization controls and review operational evidence in your own environment.
problem: Your response tooling must fit your data handling, access and retention requirements.
workflow: Plan the deployment, configure scoped roles and identity, review audit events, and use privacy and evidence workflows for your own controls.
deployment: Keep the application, database, backups, and network controls inside the environment governed by your organization. Select a topology that fits your own availability and recovery requirements.
integration: Prefer narrowly scoped provider credentials and document every inbound and outbound trust boundary used by the incident workflow.
security: Configure enterprise identity, least-privilege roles, audit evidence, secret rotation, retention, and network hardening. OpsKnight controls support your program but do not create compliance certification by themselves.
validation: Prove access denial as well as success: allowed user, denied user, audit event capture, credential rotation, backup/restore, and incident evidence retention.

label: On-call operations
headline: Make responsibility explicit.
description: Build schedules, apply overrides and route escalation to the responder responsible for the service.
problem: Coverage and handoffs are hard to reason about during a page.
workflow: Create rotations, validate current coverage, configure escalation targets and confirm delivery outcomes on a test incident.
deployment: The deployment choice matters less than proving the scheduler, worker health, database durability, and notification-provider reachability during an incident.
integration: Map services to the schedules and escalation policies that actually own them. Enable only the paging channels responders are expected to use and test each configured provider.
security: Limit schedule and escalation administration to the roles that need it, and protect notification-provider credentials with the same production secret controls as the rest of the platform.
validation: Test current coverage, an override, a triggered incident, each required delivery channel, acknowledgement, retry visibility, and escalation behavior.

label: DevOps teams
headline: Connect your monitoring to the response.
description: Bring signals from your existing tools into a shared incident lifecycle.
problem: Alerts arrive from several tools, while ownership and communication happen elsewhere.
workflow: Connect providers, map services and escalation policies, coordinate in ChatOps and publish scoped customer updates.
deployment: Begin with a simple integrated deployment for evaluation, then choose split or Kubernetes based on the production availability and operations model rather than team size alone.
integration: Connect monitoring and delivery systems already in use, route alerts by service ownership, use ChatOps for coordination, and publish only customer-safe updates to status pages.
security: Configure identity, roles, API keys, provider credentials, HTTPS, backups, and audit review before treating the installation as production incident infrastructure.
validation: Send representative alerts from each important source and verify deduplication, assignment, paging, ChatOps actions, status communication, resolution, and recovery.
